blocks.content: An orphan process is the mirror image of the zombie covered in the previous chapter. A zombie is a child that has finished but has not yet been collected by its still living parent. An orphan is the opposite: a child that is still very much running, but whose parent has already exited out from underneath it.

Unlike a zombie buildup, which signals a genuine bug in a poorly written parent, orphaning is a completely routine, expected event that the kernel handles automatically and gracefully, and it underlies one of the most common patterns in Unix system administration, the background daemon.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-787305166.png
1. What an Orphan Process Actually Is
blocks.text: 1. What an Orphan Process Actually Is

blocks.content: An orphan process is simply a running child process whose original parent has already terminated. Nothing about the child itself changes when this happens, it keeps executing exactly the same code it was already running, with exactly the same resources. The only thing that changes is who its parent process is considered to be.

This is a fundamentally different situation from a zombie. A zombie has already finished and is just waiting on bookkeeping. An orphan is fully alive and running, it has simply lost the specific process that originally created it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-680271426.png
blocks.alt: What an Orphan Process Actually Is

blocks.content: 2. Why the Kernel Immediately Reparents It
blocks.text: 2. Why the Kernel Immediately Reparents It

blocks.content: The wait mechanism from the zombie chapter fundamentally depends on a process having a parent, since collecting a finished child exit status is specifically the parent job. A process left with genuinely no parent at all would have no one able to ever call wait on it, meaning it would inevitably become an uncollectable zombie the instant it eventually finished.

To prevent this, the kernel does not allow a process to ever truly have no parent. The moment a process becomes orphaned, the kernel immediately reassigns it a new parent, so there is always someone available to eventually collect its exit status when it does finish.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-623522874.png
blocks.alt: Why the Kernel Immediately Reparents It

blocks.title: A guarantee, not an exception
blocks.content: The kernel treats having a parent as a guarantee every process can rely on. Orphaning never leaves a process truly parentless, even momentarily, reparenting happens as an immediate, atomic part of the exiting parent own shutdown sequence.
3. Before and After: Watching the Reparenting Happen
blocks.text: 3. Before and After: Watching the Reparenting Happen

blocks.content: Concretely, consider a parent process with PID 500 that has spawned a child with PID 800. That child parent PID, PPID, field correctly shows 500, reflecting the real relationship. The moment the parent with PID 500 exits, the child does not disappear or stop running, it simply gets its PPID field rewritten.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-469738876.png
blocks.alt: Before and After: Watching the Reparenting Happen

blocks.content: 4. init: The Traditional Universal Adopter

On traditional Unix and Linux systems, orphaned processes are reparented to init, the very first process the kernel starts at boot, always assigned PID 1. init role includes automatically adopting every orphaned process in the entire system, regardless of what that process is or was originally doing.

Because init is a long lived, carefully written system process, it periodically calls wait on all of its adopted children, meaning orphaned processes that eventually finish running get properly collected and do not linger as permanent zombies either. init effectively acts as a safety net for both halves of the parent child relationship problem this pair of chapters covers.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-686222110.png
Modern systems: systemd and subreapers

Most modern Linux distributions use systemd rather than the traditional init, filling exactly the same PID 1 adoption role. Additionally, Linux supports a subreaper mechanism, where a long running application, a container runtime is the classic example, can mark itself to receive its own orphaned descendants directly, rather than having them jump all the way up to PID 1.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409296227-473872504.png

5. Orphaning Is Usually Completely Intentional

Unlike zombie buildup, which is always a sign of a bug, orphaning happens constantly on any real system and is very often entirely intentional. The most familiar everyday example is starting a background process from a terminal and then closing that terminal window entirely.

The background process does not get killed just because the shell that originally launched it has exited. It simply becomes an orphan, gets reparented to init or a subreaper, and keeps running exactly as before, now fully independent of the terminal session that started it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297578-832650902.png
6. The Double Fork Pattern: Deliberately Creating a Daemon
blocks.text: 6. The Double Fork Pattern: Deliberately Creating a Daemon

blocks.content: Orphaning is not just something that happens by accident, Unix system programming actually relies on it deliberately through a well known technique called the double fork, the classic way to turn an ordinary program into a fully independent background daemon.

The original process forks once, producing a child. That child immediately forks again, producing a grandchild, and then the first child exits right away. The grandchild, now parentless the instant its own immediate parent exited, becomes an orphan and gets reparented straight up to init. The result is a process guaranteed to never become a zombie under its original ancestor, fully detached and independently supervised by init from that point forward.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409297579-334368345.png
blocks.alt: The Double Fork Pattern: Deliberately Creating a Daemon

8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Confusing an orphan with a zombie, since both terms sound negative, when an orphan is a completely healthy running process and a zombie is an already finished one waiting on collection.","Assuming an orphaned process gets killed automatically when its parent exits, when in reality it is simply reparented and keeps running exactly as before.","Not recognizing the double fork pattern as a deliberate, intentional use of orphaning to build an independent daemon, rather than something to avoid."]
items: Confusing an orphan with a zombie, since both terms sound negative, when an orphan is a completely healthy running process and a zombie is an already finished one waiting on collection.
Assuming an orphaned process gets killed automatically when its parent exits, when in reality it is simply reparented and keeps running exactly as before.
Not recognizing the double fork pattern as a deliberate, intentional use of orphaning to build an independent daemon, rather than something to avoid.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to state the core distinction cleanly: an orphan is alive but has lost its parent, a zombie is dead but has not yet been collected by its parent. Also be ready to explain the double fork technique and why it reliably produces a fully independent daemon process.

Together, this pair of chapters covers both ends of what can happen to a parent child relationship after fork: a finished child waiting to be collected, and a still running child that has outlived its parent. Both are handled gracefully by the kernel, one through the zombie mechanism, the other through automatic reparenting.
